title: One hand, many notes
teaches: The arpeggiator: modes, octave range, rate, swing and hold

blocks.text: **The sound.** Here are four chords, each held for a bar, played through a short pluck. Then the same four chords, held the same way, but now each comes out as a running stream of notes, faster and wider than one hand could play. Nobody played the stream. The synth did.

blocks.caption: Four chords held, then the same chords through the arpeggiator

blocks.text: The machine doing it is an **arpeggiator**. It takes the notes you hold and plays them one at a time, in an order, at a steady rate, for as long as you hold them. An arpeggio is a chord played one note at a time, as a harpist does; the word comes from the Italian for playing the harp.[^harp]

An arpeggiator has a handful of settings, and the first is the **order**. **Up** plays the held notes from the lowest to the highest, then starts again. **Down** goes the other way. **Order** plays them in the order the keys went down, so the same chord can give different patterns. **Random** picks a held note at each step. **Octaves** repeats the pattern one, two or three octaves higher before going round again, which is how a small chord becomes a wide sweep.

blocks.caption: A held chord of three notes, as the arpeggiator plays it over one bar.
blocks.task: Try three modes, and two octaves or more

blocks.text: The **rate** is how many notes fit in a beat, and like the LFO's rate it is counted against the tempo: eighth notes, sixteenths, thirty-seconds. An arpeggiator is therefore always in time with whatever else is playing, which is what made it so useful in dance music.
Below, the arpeggiator is off and the loop holds its chords. Switch it on and try its settings. Then stop the loop and hold three keys on the keyboard: the arpeggiator plays whatever you hold.

blocks.caption: A short pluck on four held chords. Switch the arpeggiator on.

blocks.text: A single held note works too: with one note and three octaves, Up gives a rising run of octaves. Most arpeggiators also have a **swing** setting, which delays every second step a little so the pattern lopes instead of ticking. You will meet swing properly with the sequencer in the next lesson.

The last setting frees your hand. With **Hold** on, the arpeggiator keeps playing the last chord after you let go, until you play a new one; then it starts on that. Keys pressed while another is still down add to the chord instead. A player can set a pattern going with one hand and spend both on the knobs.

blocks.caption: The arpeggiator on, from the keyboard. Switch Hold on, play a chord and let go.

blocks.text: With Hold on, the arpeggiator becomes a crude sequencer: a pattern that plays itself while you change the sound. Sweeping the cutoff or the envelope amount over a running arpeggio is one of the oldest moves in synth music. The arpeggiator follows the tempo of the synth's clock, and two machines that share a clock stay together.[^clock]
Now make the arpeggio from the start of this lesson. The pluck is holding its chords again. Make the notes run upwards over two octaves, in sixteenth notes.

blocks.caption: Four held chords. Make them run.

blocks.text: When you meet an arpeggiator on a strange synth, there is usually a button to switch it on, a Hold button, and the rest (order, octaves, rate, swing) on a shared knob or a menu. If a synth plays a stream of notes when you press one key, or keeps playing after you let go, the arpeggiator and its Hold are the first things to check.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the arpeggiator
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

choices: Plays the held notes one at a time, in an order, at a steady rate
Plays a chord from one key
items.why: It turns held notes into a stream.

items.ask: Mode Up, one octave, holding C, E and G. What plays?
choices: C E G C E G ...
G E C G E C ...
items.why: Up goes from lowest to highest, then starts again.

items.ask: What does the Octaves setting do?
choices: Repeats the pattern higher before going round
items.why: Two octaves plays the held notes, then the same an octave up.

items.ask: Why is the arpeggiator's rate given in note lengths like 1/16?
choices: It is counted against the tempo, so it stays in time
It is a fixed number of hertz
It is the length of the release
items.why: A synced rate follows the tempo, like the LFO's.

items.ask: The synth keeps playing a pattern after you let go of the keys. Which setting is on?
items.why: Hold keeps the last chord going until a new one is played.

summary: **An arpeggiator plays held notes one at a time**, in an order, at a steady rate.
**Up, Down, Order and Random** decide the order; Order follows the keys as they went down.
**Octaves repeats the pattern higher**, so a small chord becomes a wide sweep.
**The rate is counted against the tempo**, so an arpeggio is always in time.
**Swing delays every second step** so a pattern lopes instead of ticking.
**Hold keeps the last chord playing** after you let go, leaving both hands free for the knobs.
**A stream of notes from one key** on a strange synth usually means the arpeggiator is on.

harp.title: Machines that arpeggiate
harp.text: Arpeggios are as old as the harp, and keyboard players have always used them to keep a held chord moving. Electronic arpeggiators arrived in the 1970s on polyphonic synths, where scanning the held keys in turn was something the keyboard's circuits already did. Roland's Jupiter-4 of 1978 had one, and by the early 1980s most synths with a microprocessor did.

clock.title: Sharing a clock
clock.text: An arpeggiator steps on a clock, and the clock can come from outside. Synths, drum machines and sequencers send one another clock pulses, usually twenty-four per beat: over a DIN cable as MIDI clock, or on older Roland gear as a separate sync signal. The machine that sends the clock sets the tempo, and every machine following it steps in time.
